slides.title: One executable can support several independent lives
keyPoints: Executable file: instructions and data on storage
Process: active resources, mappings, and execution
slides.narration: A program file is a recipe; a process is one operating-system-managed use of that recipe. Two editor windows can execute the same program while keeping different documents and descriptor tables. A thread is an execution stream within the process, with its own registers and stack. This distinction matters when diagnosing a slow service: is the task waiting for input, competing for a processor, or sharing a lock with another thread? Adding more copies of the executable does not answer that question. Name the resource and execution state before suggesting a scheduling change. Our first demonstration creates a real child process and checks a private-memory relationship.

slides.title: A real child changes its private value
keyPoints: fork creates a child process on Linux/POSIX
Parent collects status with waitpid
Only the parent prints, so output order is stable
slides.narration: This program uses actual process creation rather than a map labeled process. Fork returns zero in the child and a child identifier in the parent. The child changes its local value from seven to nine and exits successfully. The parent waits for that exact child, retrying if waiting was interrupted, then prints its own unchanged seven and the child status zero. No process identifier or timing assumption appears in the expected output. Waitpid also collects the child termination record. The example establishes private modification and status collection; it does not measure physical page copying or prove how the kernel implements that isolation.

slides.title: Runnable is a permission, not current execution
keyPoints: Ready means eligible to run
Waiting means an event is still needed
A wakeup need not preempt the current task
slides.narration: Consider one processor currently running B while A waits for input. When A receives input, it becomes ready. That does not automatically give it the processor or make B stop. Running describes actual execution; ready describes eligibility; waiting describes a missing prerequisite. Confusing these states can produce a scheduler model with two running tasks on one processor. A terminated child waiting to be collected is different again: its old program is no longer running. The remaining record lets a parent retrieve status. These names are simplified, but the distinctions remain useful when reading real system diagnostics or explaining why a waiting job has little CPU usage.

question.answer: No. Wakeup makes it eligible; scheduling decides when it runs.

slides.title: Reject dispatch while another task owns the CPU
keyPoints: This is a state model, not an OS scheduler
Wakeup changes Waiting to Ready
Dispatch requires an idle modeled CPU
slides.narration: The modeled CPU initially belongs to B, so dispatching A must fail even after A becomes ready. The first printed false comes from trying to dispatch A while it still waits. Wakeup then returns true and changes only A to ready. A second dispatch still returns false because the CPU owner is B. Once B is explicitly removed from the modeled CPU, dispatch succeeds. The final true confirms both A’s running state and its ownership of the CPU. This adds an invariant the generic source transition helper cannot enforce by itself: at most one task runs on this modeled processor.

slides.narration: The process abstraction groups resources and identity. Its virtual address space determines which addresses have meaning; its descriptor table determines what small descriptor numbers refer to; its credentials help determine which requests are allowed. Two processes can use the integer descriptor 3 for entirely different files. A thread is an execution stream within that environment. Threads in one process usually share mappings and many resources while retaining their own register state and stacks. The scheduler chooses runnable execution entities, while the process abstraction supplies much of their shared environment.

slides.narration: A simple state model includes running, runnable, waiting, stopped, and terminated states. Runnable means eligible for CPU execution; running means currently executing. A process waiting for input is not made faster merely by adding more CPU time if the required input has not arrived. A terminated child may temporarily remain as a zombie until its parent collects the termination information. The zombie is not executing the old program. Its remaining bookkeeping supports the parent’s ability to retrieve status. Real kernels expose more detailed states than this teaching model, but the model is sufficient to separate eligibility, execution, and event waiting.

slides.title: Address space
slides.eyebrow: SOURCE CONCEPT · REASON THROUGH THE MECHANISM
keyPoints: An address space defines the virtual mappings visible to a process.
It contains executable code, data, stacks, dynamically allocated regions, shared mappings, and reserved or inaccessible gaps.
Two processes can map different physical storage at the same virtual address.
Conversely, two processes can map the same physical storage at different virtual addresses.
slides.narration:
An address space defines the virtual mappings visible to a process. It contains executable code, data, stacks, dynamically allocated regions, shared mappings, and reserved or inaccessible gaps. Two processes can map different physical storage at the same virtual address. Conversely, two processes can map the same physical storage at different virtual addresses. This is how shared mappings can coexist with otherwise distinct address spaces. A pointer stored in shared memory is therefore not automatically meaningful in another process. Use offsets or another explicitly designed representation when the same region may appear at different base addresses.

In plain English: Think of an address written on a note: the note can tell you where to look, but it does not prove the thing is still there or that you are allowed to use it.

slides.title: Context switching
slides.eyebrow: SOURCE CONCEPT · REASON THROUGH THE MECHANISM
keyPoints: A context switch changes which execution stream uses a processor.
It requires saving and restoring relevant state and may involve changing the active address-space context.
Switching between threads in the same process can avoid some address-space changes, but it still has scheduling and execution-state costs.
The effects extend beyond the instructions that perform the switch.
slides.narration: A context switch changes which execution stream uses a processor. It requires saving and restoring relevant state and may involve changing the active address-space context. Switching between threads in the same process can avoid some address-space changes, but it still has scheduling and execution-state costs. The effects extend beyond the instructions that perform the switch. A different working set can displace useful cache entries or translations. Conversely, a context switch does not imply that all caches are universally flushed. Actual hardware and kernel mechanisms determine which state remains useful. Avoid reducing context-switch cost to one supposedly universal number.

slides.title: A scheduling model with waiting
slides.eyebrow: SOURCE CONCEPT · REASON THROUGH THE MECHANISM
keyPoints: Assume one CPU, zero switching overhead, and a scheduler that gives a newly runnable job the next available opportunity.
Job A needs 2 milliseconds of CPU, then waits 5 milliseconds for I/O, then needs 1 millisecond of CPU.
Job B needs 4 milliseconds of CPU and never blocks.

slides.narration: Assume one CPU, zero switching overhead, and a scheduler that gives a newly runnable job the next available opportunity. Job A needs 2 milliseconds of CPU, then waits 5 milliseconds for I/O, then needs 1 millisecond of CPU. Job B needs 4 milliseconds of CPU and never blocks. Both are ready at time zero, and A starts first. A consumes 3 milliseconds of CPU but finishes after 8 milliseconds of wall time. B consumes 4 milliseconds and finishes at time 6. The CPU performs 7 milliseconds of useful work during an 8-millisecond observation interval, giving modeled utilization of 7 / 8 = 87.5% . This calculation assumes that the I/O wait completes at time 7 independently of B. It excludes kernel work, interrupt overhead, and real scheduling details. The point is not to predict a production trace but to establish the vocabulary and accounting needed to interpret one.

slides.title: A saved context is more than local variables
keyPoints: Resume requires instruction and stack positions
Registers and flags carry live execution state
A context switch must preserve each stream’s meaning
slides.narration: Suppose A is paused between computing a sum and storing it. The current instruction position, stack position, registers, and relevant flags help define what happens next. Saving only named source variables is insufficient because the compiler may keep values in registers or remove variables entirely. The kernel preserves the architecture-defined execution context needed to resume correctly. A context switch may also change the active address-space context when the new stream belongs to another process. That is different from a function call, whose calling convention divides preservation duties between caller and callee. Do not diagnose a context-switch error by assuming every source variable occupies one stack slot.
actions: Ask learners to answer the question with a concrete state or calculation before revealing the explanation.

question.prompt: Why is saving an integer array of source variables not a complete context switch?
question.answer: Execution also depends on instruction location, stack state, flags, and other architecture-defined register state.

slides.title: CPU time and elapsed time answer different questions
keyPoints: A uses 3 units of CPU across 8 elapsed units
B executes while A waits
Utilization needs an explicit observation interval
slides.narration: In the chapter’s model, A runs from time zero to two, waits until seven, then runs until eight. B runs from two to six. The processor is idle from six to seven, so useful CPU work totals seven units during eight elapsed units: eighty-seven point five percent utilization. A’s own CPU time is only three units, although its completion takes eight. These are model units under stated assumptions, not measurements from our machine. Changing the I/O duration changes elapsed time without changing A’s required computation. When comparing real programs, report whether a number measures wall time, one process’s CPU time, or total CPU work across workers.

slides.title: Isolation permits deliberate communication
keyPoints: Equal address numbers can name different storage
Shared mappings and descriptors require explicit contracts
A pointer is not a portable cross-process identifier
slides.narration: The number three can be a descriptor for a log in one process and a socket in another. Likewise, the same virtual address can map unrelated physical storage. Sending either number to another process does not automatically transfer the resource it names. An intentional communication channel needs a representation and a lifetime rule. For shared regions, an offset from a known base can be meaningful even when each process maps the region at a different address. Isolation also does not prevent competition for processor time or memory bandwidth. Separate what processes may directly access from which physical resources they compete to use.
actions: Ask learners to answer the question with a concrete state or calculation before revealing the explanation.

question.prompt: Does sending a numeric pointer to another process make the pointed-to object available there?
question.answer: No. Its meaning depends on the sender’s mappings and object lifetime; the receiver needs an explicit shared representation.

slides.title: Process completion includes collecting the result
keyPoints: Termination ends execution
Waiting collects child status
Resource ownership continues across error paths
slides.narration: A child can finish before its parent looks at the result. The kernel retains enough termination information for the parent to collect it; that remaining record is often called a zombie. It is not a hidden worker still executing the old program. Our fork demonstration waits for the exact child and checks that termination was normal before reading an exit code. This ordering matters because a signal termination has a different status representation. In a server that repeatedly launches children, forgetting collection can accumulate records even when every child’s work completed. Review creation and collection as one lifecycle, including error and cancellation paths.

question.prompt: Why check WIFEXITED before WEXITSTATUS?
question.answer: The exit-code interpretation applies to normal exit; termination by a signal has different status information.

slides.title: Scheduling policy cannot repair a missing event
keyPoints: Investigate blocking before increasing priority
Context-switch cost depends on workload and hardware
Caches are not universally emptied by every switch
slides.narration: If a worker waits for a client request that has not arrived, a higher scheduling priority cannot manufacture that input. If many workers are runnable, priorities instead decide who receives scarce execution time. Context switches also have indirect costs because the newly running work may use different cache lines or translations. That does not mean every switch flushes every cache. Hardware and kernel mechanisms vary, and some state remains useful. For maintenance, collect evidence about runnable demand, actual execution, and reasons for blocking before adjusting thread counts. A single average CPU percentage cannot explain which of these limits dominates.

slides.title: Defend a process model with explicit invariants
keyPoints: Separate program identity, execution state, and resources
Keep one CPU owner in the one-core model
Test rejection as well as successful transitions
slides.narration: A useful process explanation follows four things: which program image is installed, what mappings and resources belong to the process, which thread can run, and what event changes its state. The source example introduces ready, running, and waiting with strings; the lab improves their representation with an enum. Our added dispatcher also tracks processor ownership. None is a complete kernel scheduler. Each model should say which rules it enforces and which it leaves to its caller. Extend the model by adding two CPUs only after stating whether each task may run on one CPU at a time. Otherwise an extra enum value can hide a broken ownership rule.
